body:
In pure water (hypotonic fluid) loss there is ...

I. increased ECF osmolality
II. decreased ECF volume
III. decreased ECF tonicity

options.hint: Check statement I and II and III.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Loss of **pure water** concentrates the ECF: **osmolality (tonicity) rises** (hypernatraemia) and water moves out of cells, so both ECF and ICF volumes **fall** (ECF volume is relatively preserved). Tonicity therefore increases, not decreases.

## Simplified explanation

Losing water makes the blood more concentrated and slightly lowers volume – I and II.

body:
High anion gap metabolic acidosis is...

I. due to depletion of bicarbonate in salicylate poisoning
II. caused by chloride depletion in diarrhoea
III. due to the increased consumption of bicarbonate in lactic acidosis
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**High anion gap** acidosis arises when an acid with an **unmeasured anion** consumes bicarbonate: lactate, ketoacids, **salicylate**, methanol, ethylene glycol, uraemia. **Diarrhoea** causes bicarbonate loss with **chloride retention** – a **normal anion gap** (hyperchloraemic) acidosis.

## Simplified explanation

Salicylate and lactic acidosis raise the anion gap; diarrhoea does not.

body:
Isotonic fluid loss can be caused by...

I. Haemorrhage
II. Vomiting and diarrhoea
III. Profuse sweating

options.hint: Check statement I and II and III.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Isotonic** loss (salt and water in plasma proportions) occurs with **haemorrhage**, burns exudate, **GI losses** (diarrhoea, vomiting, fistulae) and third spacing. **Sweat** is hypotonic, so profuse sweating causes predominantly water loss.

## Simplified explanation

Bleeding and GI losses are isotonic; sweat is watery.

body:
Metabolic alkalosis can be caused by ...

I. The gain of bicarbonate
II. Loss of hydrogen
III. Loss of chloride
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Metabolic alkalosis results from **gain of bicarbonate** (antacids, bicarbonate infusion), **loss of H⁺** (vomiting, mineralocorticoid excess) and is maintained by **chloride depletion** (contraction alkalosis) and hypokalaemia.

## Simplified explanation

All three cause metabolic alkalosis.

body:
The causes of respiratory acidosis include...

I. Physical inability to ventilate
II. Asthma
III. Head injury
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Respiratory acidosis** (CO₂ retention) follows **hypoventilation**: chest wall/neuromuscular disease (inability to ventilate), airway obstruction (severe **asthma**, COPD) and **CNS depression** (head injury, drugs).

## Simplified explanation

All three can stop you breathing out CO₂ properly.

body:
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) is associated with...

I. Increased ECF osmolality
II. Increased urine sodium excretion
III. Increased activity of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In **SIADH**, water retention **lowers** plasma osmolality (dilutional hyponatraemia) while the urine is inappropriately concentrated. Mild volume expansion increases **ANP** and suppresses aldosterone, causing **natriuresis (urine Na > 30 mmol/L)**.

## Simplified explanation

SIADH: low osmolality, salty urine and more ANP – II and III.

body:
In isotonic fluid overload there is ...

I. Increased ECF osmolality
II. Hypertension
III. Normal ECF osmolality
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Isotonic overload** (retention of salt and water together, e.g. heart failure, renal failure, excess saline) expands the ECF with **normal osmolality**, producing oedema and **hypertension**.

## Simplified explanation

Extra salt-and-water raises blood pressure but keeps osmolality normal.

body:
In interpreting chemical pathology results, ______ of the patient must be considered.

I. Date of birth
II. Posture
III. Marital status

options.hint: Check statement I and II and III.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Age (from **date of birth**), sex, **posture** (upright posture raises protein-bound analytes, renin, aldosterone), time of day, diet, pregnancy and drugs affect results. Marital status has no physiological effect.

## Simplified explanation

Age and posture matter; marital status doesn't.

body:
The following are considered as pre-analytical sources of error in the clinical chemistry laboratory...

I. Failure to analyse controls
II. Not using appropriate volumes for test procedure
III. Taking sample meant for electrolyte into EDTA tubes

options.hint: Check statement I and II and III.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Pre-analytical** errors occur before analysis: wrong patient/label, wrong **tube** (K₂EDTA raises K⁺ and lowers Ca²⁺), haemolysis, delayed transport, wrong timing. Failing to run **controls** and wrong **pipetting volumes** are **analytical** errors.

## Simplified explanation

Only the wrong tube is pre-analytical.

body:
Causes of glucosuria include ...

I. Diabetes insipidus
II. Diabetes mellitus
III. Renal tubular dysfunction
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Glucosuria** occurs when filtered glucose exceeds the renal threshold (**diabetes mellitus**, other hyperglycaemia) or tubular reabsorption is defective (**renal glycosuria**, Fanconi syndrome, SGLT2 inhibitors, pregnancy). Diabetes insipidus causes dilute polyuria without glucose.

## Simplified explanation

Diabetes mellitus and tubular disorders cause glucose in urine; diabetes insipidus does not.

body:
Causes of oliguria include ...

I. Renal ischaemia
II. Acute kidney injury
III. Burns
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Oliguria** (< 400 mL/day) occurs with reduced renal perfusion (hypovolaemia from **burns**, haemorrhage; **renal ischaemia**), **acute kidney injury** and urinary obstruction.

## Simplified explanation

All three reduce urine output.

body:
Age-related differences affect the interpretation of ...

I. Total bilirubin
II. Conjugated bilirubin
III. Alkaline phosphatase
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Total (unconjugated) bilirubin** is physiologically high in **neonates**; **alkaline phosphatase** is much higher in **growing children/adolescents** (bone growth). Conjugated bilirubin is normally low at all ages – a raised level is always abnormal.

## Simplified explanation

Total bilirubin (newborns) and ALP (children) vary with age.

body:
Time of day affects the interpretation of the serum concentrations of ....

I. Glycated haemoglobin
II. Cortisol
III. Iron
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Cortisol** (peak ~9 am, trough at midnight) and **serum iron** (higher in the morning) show **diurnal variation**. **HbA1c** reflects 2–3 months of glycaemia and is unaffected by time of day.

## Simplified explanation

Cortisol and iron vary through the day; HbA1c doesn't.

body:
Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis:

I. Is a common occurrence in patients with hypoalbuminaemia
II. In renal tubular acidosis is due to increased loss of hydrogen ions
III. In diarrhoea is due to increased reabsorption of chloride

options.hint: Check statement I and II and III.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic)** acidosis results from bicarbonate loss (**diarrhoea**, proximal RTA) or failure of H⁺ excretion (distal RTA), with compensatory **chloride retention**. Hypoalbuminaemia **lowers** the anion gap and can mask a high-gap acidosis. In RTA, the defect is **retention** (reduced excretion) of H⁺ or loss of HCO₃⁻, not increased H⁺ loss.

## Simplified explanation

Only the diarrhoea statement is correct.

body:
Consider the following statements on compensation in acid-base disorders

I. Compensation is partial when pH remains unchanged in spite of normal CO₂ or bicarbonate
II. Altered rate of breathing compensates for metabolic disorders
III. The part of the body that compensates for the disorder is not affected by the primary disease
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Compensation is **complete** (fully compensated) when pH returns to normal; **partial** when pH is still abnormal. **Respiratory** compensation (changing ventilation) corrects **metabolic** disorders; **renal** compensation corrects respiratory ones. The compensating system must itself be unaffected by the primary disease.

## Simplified explanation

II and III are true; statement I describes complete, not partial, compensation.

body:
Hypoalbuminaemia due to increased loss can be caused by...

I. Protein losing enteropathy
II. Nephrotic syndrome
III. Acute tubular necrosis

options.hint: Check statement I and II and III.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Albumin is **lost** through the gut (**protein-losing enteropathy**), the kidney (**nephrotic syndrome** – glomerular proteinuria) and skin (burns). **Acute tubular necrosis** causes only mild tubular proteinuria.

## Simplified explanation

Gut and nephrotic losses lower albumin; ATN does not.

body:
Acute phase proteins (reactants):

I. Are increased or decreased in chronic inflammation
II. Albumin is a positive acute phase protein as it increases in inflammation
III. Help to fight the growth of microorganisms
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Acute phase proteins** change in **acute and chronic** inflammation: **positive** (CRP, SAA, fibrinogen, haptoglobin, α1-antitrypsin, caeruloplasmin) increase; **negative** (**albumin**, transferrin, prealbumin) decrease. Many have antimicrobial roles (CRP opsonises, complement activation, iron sequestration).

## Simplified explanation

I and III are true; albumin is a negative acute phase protein.

body:
Albumin is useful in the....

I. assessment of hydration status
II. adjustment of serum calcium levels
III. investigation of kwashiorkor
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Albumin** rises with **dehydration** (haemoconcentration), is used to **correct total calcium** (corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.02 × (40 − albumin)), and is low in protein malnutrition such as **kwashiorkor**.

## Simplified explanation

All three uses are correct.

body:
Serum protein electrophoresis:

I. Separates proteins based on their charges and size
II. Provides a qualitative profile of plasma proteins
III. Gamma globulins give a single (narrow) band in the healthy state

options.hint: Check statement I and II and III.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

SPE separates proteins mainly by **charge** (and size/shape) into albumin, α1, α2, β and γ zones, giving a **qualitative/semi-quantitative** profile. In health the **γ-globulins are polyclonal**, producing a **broad diffuse** band – a narrow band suggests a monoclonal paraprotein.

## Simplified explanation

I and II are true; normal gamma globulins form a broad band.

body:
Diabetic ketoacidosis causes high anion gap metabolic acidosis due to

I. Hydrogen ion retention
II. Bicarbonate depletion
III. Retention of ketoanions
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Acetoacetic and β-hydroxybutyric acids dissociate, adding **H⁺** (which consumes/depletes **bicarbonate**) and leaving unmeasured **ketoanions**, which raise the anion gap.

## Simplified explanation

All three contribute to the high anion gap acidosis of DKA.

body:
Causes of pseudohyperkalaemia:

I. Myeloproliferative disorders
II. Metabolic acidosis
III. Severe thrombocytosis
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Pseudohyperkalaemia** is an in-vitro rise in K⁺: haemolysis, delayed separation, EDTA contamination, fist clenching, **thrombocytosis** and **leucocytosis/myeloproliferative disorders** (K⁺ released from cells during clotting). **Metabolic acidosis** causes a true shift of K⁺ out of cells.

## Simplified explanation

Lots of platelets or white cells release K⁺ in the tube; acidosis is a true rise.

body:
Consider the following statements on hypokalaemia. Hypokalaemia...

I. Can lead to glucose intolerance
II. Affects gastrointestinal tract (GIT) muscles and will lead to constipation
III. Can result from magnesium deficiency
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Hypokalaemia** impairs **insulin secretion** (glucose intolerance), causes smooth and skeletal muscle weakness (**constipation/ileus**, paralysis), arrhythmias and nephrogenic DI. **Magnesium deficiency** causes renal K⁺ wasting and refractory hypokalaemia.

## Simplified explanation

All three statements are true.

body:
In multiple myeloma;

I. There is elevated ESR
II. There is hypoalbuminaemia
III. The elevated ESR is due to decreased haemoglobin concentration

options.hint: Check statement I and II and III.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In **myeloma**, the high **paraprotein** promotes **rouleaux** formation and a **markedly raised ESR**; albumin is often **reduced** (compensatory and disease-related). Anaemia contributes slightly, but the main cause of the high ESR is the paraprotein.

## Simplified explanation

High ESR and low albumin – but the ESR is from the paraprotein, not anaemia.

body:
Acute phase proteins:

I. All acute phase proteins are elevated immediately after an infection
II. Haptoglobin is elevated 24–48 hours after an inflammatory response
III. C reactive protein is the first to be elevated after an inflammatory response
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

APPs rise at different speeds: **CRP** and SAA rise first (within **6–12 h**, peak ~48 h); α1-antitrypsin, α1-acid glycoprotein and **haptoglobin** rise after **24–48 h**; fibrinogen and caeruloplasmin later. Negative APPs fall.

## Simplified explanation

CRP rises first; haptoglobin follows after a day or two; not all rise at once.

body: Match the cause with the acid-base imbalance it produces: **Muscle paralysis**

options.hint: Correct. Respiratory muscle paralysis causes hypoventilation and CO₂ retention → **respiratory acidosis**.

hint: Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Respiratory muscle paralysis causes hypoventilation and CO₂ retention → **respiratory acidosis**.

## Simplified explanation

Can't breathe properly → CO₂ builds up.

body: Match the cause with the acid-base imbalance it produces: **Chronic obstructive airway disease**

options.hint: Correct. COPD causes chronic CO₂ retention → (compensated) **respiratory acidosis**.

hint: Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

COPD causes chronic CO₂ retention → (compensated) **respiratory acidosis**.

## Simplified explanation

COPD traps CO₂ → respiratory acidosis.

body: Match the cause with the acid-base imbalance it produces: **Use of antacids**

options.hint: Correct. Excess alkali (bicarbonate, milk-alkali) ingestion → **metabolic alkalosis**.

hint: Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Excess alkali (bicarbonate, milk-alkali) ingestion → **metabolic alkalosis**.

## Simplified explanation

Swallowing alkali → metabolic alkalosis.

body: Match the cause with the acid-base imbalance it produces: **Hyperaldosteronism**

options.hint: Correct. Aldosterone increases distal H⁺ and K⁺ secretion and bicarbonate generation → hypokalaemic **metabolic alkalosis**.

hint: Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Aldosterone increases distal H⁺ and K⁺ secretion and bicarbonate generation → hypokalaemic **metabolic alkalosis**.

## Simplified explanation

Too much aldosterone → metabolic alkalosis.

body: Match the cause with the acid-base imbalance it produces: **Ingestion of anti-freeze**

options.hint: Correct. Ethylene glycol is metabolised to glycolic and oxalic acids → **high anion gap metabolic acidosis** (with high osmolal gap).

hint: Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Ethylene glycol is metabolised to glycolic and oxalic acids → **high anion gap metabolic acidosis** (with high osmolal gap).

## Simplified explanation

Antifreeze makes acids → high anion gap acidosis.

body: Match the cause with the acid-base imbalance it produces: **Vomiting**

options.hint: Correct. Loss of gastric HCl and volume/chloride depletion → **metabolic alkalosis**.

hint: Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Loss of gastric HCl and volume/chloride depletion → **metabolic alkalosis**.

## Simplified explanation

Vomiting loses acid → metabolic alkalosis.

body: Match the cause with the acid-base imbalance it produces: **Vomiting and chronic obstructive lung disease**

options.hint: Correct. Metabolic alkalosis (vomiting) plus respiratory acidosis (COPD) → **mixed disorder**.

hint: Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Metabolic alkalosis (vomiting) plus respiratory acidosis (COPD) → **mixed disorder**.

## Simplified explanation

Two processes together → mixed.

body: Match the cause with the acid-base imbalance it produces: **Vomiting and lactic acidosis**

options.hint: Correct. Metabolic alkalosis plus high anion gap metabolic acidosis → **mixed disorder**.

hint: Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Metabolic alkalosis plus high anion gap metabolic acidosis → **mixed disorder**.

## Simplified explanation

Two processes together → mixed.

body: Match the cause with the electrolyte disorder: **Cirrhosis and ascites**

options.hint: Correct. Cirrhosis causes secondary hyperaldosteronism and ADH release with total body sodium and water excess (oedema/ascites) but proportionally more water → **hypervolaemic hyponatraemia**.

hint: Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Cirrhosis causes secondary hyperaldosteronism and ADH release with total body sodium and water excess (oedema/ascites) but proportionally more water → **hypervolaemic hyponatraemia**.

## Simplified explanation

Fluid overload with diluted sodium.

body: Match the cause with the electrolyte disorder: **Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (ADH)**

options.hint: Correct. Water retention without oedema → **euvolaemic (normovolaemic) hyponatraemia**.

hint: Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Water retention without oedema → **euvolaemic (normovolaemic) hyponatraemia**.

## Simplified explanation

SIADH: diluted sodium, normal volume.

body: Match the cause with the electrolyte disorder: **Psychogenic polydipsia**

options.hint: Correct. Excessive water intake exceeding renal excretory capacity → **normovolaemic (dilutional) hyponatraemia**.

hint: Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Excessive water intake exceeding renal excretory capacity → **normovolaemic (dilutional) hyponatraemia**.

## Simplified explanation

Drinking too much water dilutes sodium.

body: Match the cause with the electrolyte disorder: **Severe hyperlipidaemia**

options.hint: Correct. Lipids occupy plasma volume; indirect ISE/flame methods report falsely low sodium → **pseudohyponatraemia** (normal osmolality).

hint: Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Lipids occupy plasma volume; indirect ISE/flame methods report falsely low sodium → **pseudohyponatraemia** (normal osmolality).

## Simplified explanation

Fat in the sample gives a falsely low sodium.

body: Match the cause with the electrolyte disorder: **Conn's syndrome**

options.hint: Correct. Aldosterone excess causes sodium retention with high-normal or mildly raised sodium → **hypernatraemia**.

hint: Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Aldosterone excess causes sodium retention with high-normal or mildly raised sodium → **hypernatraemia**.

## Simplified explanation

Aldosterone excess keeps sodium high.

body:
Albumin...

a. has a half-life of 20 days
b. is unaffected by volume status
c. is increased in multiple myeloma
d. levels are reduced in acute inflammation
e. is reduced in polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. has a half-life of 20 days | **T** | About 20 days. |
| b. is unaffected by volume status | **F** | Rises in dehydration, falls with overhydration. |
| c. is increased in multiple myeloma | **F** | Usually reduced. |
| d. levels are reduced in acute inflammation | **T** | Negative acute phase protein. |
| e. is reduced in polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia | **T** | Compensatory reduction maintains oncotic pressure. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b F, c F, d T, e T.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Albumin** (half-life ~20 days, so a poor marker of acute nutritional change) is a **negative acute phase protein**, varies with **hydration**, and falls when globulins rise (myeloma, chronic infection, cirrhosis) to keep oncotic pressure steady.

## Simplified explanation

Albumin lasts ~20 days, falls in inflammation and when globulins rise, and changes with hydration.

body:
Point of care testing:....

a. Cannot be used to measure serum bilirubin
b. Test kits must be calibrated regularly by trained personnel
c. Eliminates need for training staff who use these equipment
d. Is less costly than what it costs to analyse samples in the laboratory
e. Is best established independently from the central biochemistry laboratory

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Cannot be used to measure serum bilirubin | **F** | Neonatal bilirubinometers exist. |
| b. Test kits must be calibrated regularly by trained personnel | **T** | Quality assurance is essential. |
| c. Eliminates need for training staff who use these equipment | **F** | Training and competency are required. |
| d. Is less costly than what it costs to analyse samples in the laboratory | **F** | Usually more expensive per test. |
| e. Is best established independently from the central biochemistry laboratory | **F** | It should be governed and quality-assured by the laboratory. |

> [!answer]
> a F, b T, c F, d F, e F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**POCT** gives rapid results near the patient but needs **trained, certified operators**, regular **calibration, QC and EQA**, and **laboratory oversight**; cost per test is usually higher than central laboratory testing.

## Simplified explanation

POCT still needs training, calibration and lab supervision, and costs more per test.

body:
Plasma proteins;

a. have buffering properties.
b. are all synthesised in the liver
c. transport steroid hormones in blood.
d. are essential in the metabolism of bilirubin.
e. are important components of the body's defence mechanism

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. have buffering properties. | **T** | Histidine and other ionisable groups buffer H⁺. |
| b. are all synthesised in the liver | **F** | Immunoglobulins are made by plasma cells. |
| c. transport steroid hormones in blood. | **T** | CBG, SHBG, albumin. |
| d. are essential in the metabolism of bilirubin. | **T** | Albumin transports unconjugated bilirubin to the liver. |
| e. are important components of the body's defence mechanism | **T** | Immunoglobulins, complement, APPs. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b F, c T, d T, e T.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Plasma proteins maintain **oncotic pressure**, **buffer** H⁺, **transport** hormones, drugs, bilirubin and metals, provide **defence** (immunoglobulins, complement), coagulation and enzymes. Most are made in the liver except **immunoglobulins** (plasma cells).

## Simplified explanation

Plasma proteins buffer, transport (incl. bilirubin and steroids) and defend; not all come from the liver.

body:
The protein electrophoretic pattern of serum, as compared with that of plasma, reveals a

a. normal albumin band
b. decreased albumin peak
c. broad increase of microglobulins
d. fibrinogen co-migration with alpha-2 globulins
e. fibrinogen peak between beta and gamma globulins

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. normal albumin band | **T** | Albumin is the same in serum and plasma. |
| b. decreased albumin peak | **F** | No change. |
| c. broad increase of microglobulins | **F** | No change. |
| d. fibrinogen co-migration with alpha-2 globulins | **F** | Serum has no fibrinogen. |
| e. fibrinogen peak between beta and gamma globulins | **F** | That band is seen in plasma, not serum. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b F, c F, d F, e F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Serum** is plasma minus clotting factors, mainly **fibrinogen**. Plasma electrophoresis shows a fibrinogen band between β and γ (which can mimic a paraprotein); serum lacks it. Other fractions, including albumin, are unchanged.

## Simplified explanation

Serum looks like plasma but without the fibrinogen band.

body:
The following changes occur in a urine sample left overnight on a work bench.

a. Dissolution of phosphate
b. Utilisation of glucose by bacteria
c. Oxidation of urobilinogen to urobilin
d. Conversion of porphobilinogen to porphyrin
e. Conversion of urea to ammonia, with consequent fall in pH

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. Dissolution of phosphate | **F** | Phosphates precipitate as pH rises. |
| b. Utilisation of glucose by bacteria | **T** | False-negative glucose. |
| c. Oxidation of urobilinogen to urobilin | **T** | Light/air oxidation. |
| d. Conversion of porphobilinogen to porphyrin | **T** | PBG polymerises to porphyrins/porphobilin (darkening). |
| e. Conversion of urea to ammonia, with consequent fall in pH | **F** | Ammonia makes urine alkaline (pH rises). |

> [!answer]
> a F, b T, c T, d T, e F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Standing urine changes: bacteria consume **glucose** and convert **urea → ammonia** (alkaline pH, phosphate **precipitation**, cast and cell lysis); **urobilinogen → urobilin** and **bilirubin → biliverdin** (light); **porphobilinogen** polymerises (urine darkens).

## Simplified explanation

Old urine loses glucose and urobilinogen, gets alkaline, and phosphates precipitate.

body:
A metabolic alkalosis and respiratory acidosis mixed acid-base disturbance can be caused by the following condition(s);

a. vomiting and chronic obstructive lung disease
b. chronic obstructive lung disease and diarrhoea
c. diuretic therapy and chronic obstructive lung disease
d. hyperparathyroidism and chronic obstructive lung disease
e. congestive cardiac failure and chronic obstructive lung disease

*Mark each option True (T) or False (F).*
answer:
| Option | T/F | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| a. vomiting and chronic obstructive lung disease | **T** | Vomiting → metabolic alkalosis; COPD → respiratory acidosis. |
| b. chronic obstructive lung disease and diarrhoea | **F** | Diarrhoea causes metabolic acidosis. |
| c. diuretic therapy and chronic obstructive lung disease | **T** | Loop/thiazide diuretics → metabolic alkalosis. |
| d. hyperparathyroidism and chronic obstructive lung disease | **F** | Hyperparathyroidism tends to cause mild hyperchloraemic acidosis. |
| e. congestive cardiac failure and chronic obstructive lung disease | **F** | CCF alone is not a cause of metabolic alkalosis. |

> [!answer]
> a T, b F, c T, d F, e F.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **metabolic alkalosis + respiratory acidosis** needs a cause of each: COPD (CO₂ retention) plus **vomiting** or **diuretics** (H⁺/Cl⁻ loss, contraction alkalosis). Diarrhoea and hyperparathyroidism produce metabolic acidosis.

## Simplified explanation

COPD plus vomiting or diuretics gives this mixed picture.

body:
A two-week-old baby girl had projectile vomiting since birth due to pyloric stenosis. After admission to the paediatric emergency unit, the following results were obtained:

Sodium 137 mmol/L (135–145); Potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5–5.0); Bicarbonate 40 mmol/L (24–32); Chloride 80 mmol/L (95–105); pH 7.55 (7.35–7.45); pCO₂ 6.2 kPa (4.6–6.0).

i. What do the results of the baby girl suggest?
ii. Give reasons for your suggestion in (i).
iii. Give a reason each for the observed levels of a. potassium b. chloride. *(10 marks)*
answer:
**i.** **Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with partial respiratory compensation.**

**ii.** pH is **high** (alkalaemia) with a **high bicarbonate** (primary metabolic alkalosis); **pCO₂ is slightly raised** – hypoventilation as respiratory compensation (partial, since pH remains high).

**iii.**
a. **Low potassium** – loss in vomitus is small; mainly **renal K⁺ loss**: volume depletion activates **aldosterone**, which promotes distal Na⁺ reabsorption in exchange for K⁺ (and H⁺); alkalosis also shifts K⁺ into cells and increases renal K⁺ secretion.
b. **Low chloride** – direct loss of **HCl** in gastric vomitus (pyloric obstruction means only gastric juice is lost); chloride depletion also maintains the alkalosis by limiting renal bicarbonate excretion.

> [!answer]
> Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (partially compensated) from loss of gastric HCl; low K⁺ from aldosterone-driven renal loss and cellular shift; low Cl⁻ from HCl loss.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In pyloric stenosis, loss of **HCl** generates bicarbonate; **volume and chloride depletion** and **hypokalaemia** maintain the alkalosis (paradoxical aciduria may develop). Treatment is saline with potassium.

## Simplified explanation

Vomiting stomach acid makes the baby alkalotic and low in chloride and potassium.

body:
The following biochemical results were obtained on a 54-year-old woman after surgery for ovarian cancer. Account for the abnormalities found. *(5 marks)*

| Serum | Result | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Urea | 2.0 | 2.5–6.6 mmol/L |
| Sodium | 120 | 135–150 mmol/L |
| Potassium | 2.0 | 3.6–5.0 mmol/L |
| Total CO₂ | 10.0 | 22–30 mmol/L |
| Bilirubin | 7.0 | 3–16 µmol/L |
| ALT | 11.0 | 10–50 U/L |
| ALP | 35.0 | 40–125 U/L |
| Total protein | 42.0 | 60–80 g/L |
| Calcium | 1.6 | 2.1–2.6 mmol/L |
| Glucose | 38 | 3.5–5.5 mmol/L |
answer:
Almost every analyte is **proportionally low** (urea, sodium, potassium, total CO₂, ALP, total protein, calcium) while **glucose is very high (38 mmol/L)**. This pattern is not physiological; it indicates the blood was **taken from the arm receiving an intravenous infusion of 5% dextrose (drip-arm contamination)** – the sample is **diluted** by the infusion fluid (lowering all constituents) and enriched with **glucose**.

The results should be **rejected** and a **repeat sample collected from the opposite arm** (or after stopping the infusion) before any clinical action.

> [!answer]
> Dilution of the sample by IV dextrose (drip-arm contamination): all analytes low, glucose very high – repeat from the other arm.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **pre-analytical** error must be suspected when results are physiologically incompatible. Contamination with dextrose-saline would give high glucose and near-normal sodium/chloride; with 5% dextrose all electrolytes fall.

## Simplified explanation

The sample was taken from the drip arm, so it's diluted with dextrose – repeat it.

body: A 50-year-old man was rushed to the emergency unit with dizziness, bloating, feeling light-headed, numbness or muscle spasms in the hands and feet, discomfort in the chest area, confusion, dry mouth and tingling in the arms. After assessment he was given a paper bag and asked to breathe in and out of the bag repeatedly. Explain the reason(s) for this intervention. *(5 marks)*
answer:
The symptoms indicate **hyperventilation syndrome** (e.g. anxiety/panic) causing **acute respiratory alkalosis**: excess CO₂ is blown off, pCO₂ falls and pH rises.

Alkalosis increases the binding of **ionised calcium** to albumin (H⁺ leaves albumin's binding sites), lowering **free ionised calcium** → neuromuscular irritability: **paraesthesia/tingling, numbness, carpopedal spasm (tetany)**; hypocapnia also causes **cerebral vasoconstriction** → dizziness, light-headedness, confusion.

**Re-breathing into a paper bag** makes the patient inhale their own expired air, which is rich in **CO₂**; this **raises pCO₂**, corrects the respiratory alkalosis, restores ionised calcium and relieves the symptoms. (It must not be used if hypoxia from other causes – e.g. asthma, MI, PE – is possible.)

> [!answer]
> Hyperventilation → respiratory alkalosis with low ionised calcium (tingling, spasms) and cerebral vasoconstriction; re-breathing CO₂ from a bag raises pCO₂ and corrects the alkalosis.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Respiratory alkalosis reduces ionised calcium without changing total calcium; restoring pCO₂ reverses this.

## Simplified explanation

He's breathing too fast and losing CO₂; breathing into a bag puts CO₂ back.

body:
A 60-year-old woman, a known diabetic, presented with the following biochemical abnormalities. In addition to insulin therapy she had been receiving **digoxin and thiazides** for congestive cardiac failure.

K⁺ 2.7 (3.5–4.9 mmol/L); HCO₃⁻ 17 (23–33 mmol/L); Cl⁻ 81 (98–106 mmol/L); Na⁺ 130 (135–145 mmol/L); Glucose 65 (3.4–6.1 mmol/L); pH 7.41 (7.35–7.45); pCO₂ 32 (35–45 mmHg).

a. Calculate the anion gap of the woman. *(2)*  b. What is the reason for the low potassium? *(2)*  c. What acid-base disorder is the woman suffering from? *(2)*  d. Justify your answer in (c). *(4)*
answer:
**a.** Anion gap = (Na⁺ + K⁺) − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) = (130 + 2.7) − (81 + 17) = **34.7 mmol/L** (or 32 mmol/L without K⁺) – **markedly raised** (normal ~10–20 / 8–16).

**b.** **Thiazide diuretics** cause renal potassium loss (increased distal Na⁺ delivery and secondary hyperaldosteronism), and **insulin therapy** drives K⁺ into cells; osmotic diuresis from hyperglycaemia adds to renal loss.

**c.** A **mixed disorder: high anion gap metabolic acidosis (diabetic ketoacidosis) with coexisting metabolic alkalosis** (thiazide-induced/hypochloraemic), with appropriate respiratory compensation – giving a near-normal pH.

**d.**
- Very high glucose with **raised anion gap** and low bicarbonate → **HAGMA** (ketoacidosis).
- **Delta ratio**: ΔAG ≈ 34.7 − 16 ≈ 19 (or 32 − 12 = 20), ΔHCO₃⁻ = 24 − 17 = 7; ratio ≈ 2.7 (> 2) → bicarbonate is **higher than expected** for the gap → coexisting **metabolic alkalosis**.
- **Hypochloraemia** and **hypokalaemia** are consistent with thiazide-induced metabolic alkalosis.
- pCO₂ 32 mmHg agrees with Winter's formula (1.5 × 17 + 8 = 33.5 ± 2) → appropriate respiratory compensation, no separate respiratory disorder; the opposing metabolic processes explain the **normal pH (7.41)**.

> [!answer]
> AG ≈ 35 mmol/L; low K⁺ from thiazides and insulin; mixed high anion gap metabolic acidosis (DKA) + metabolic alkalosis (thiazide), compensated, hence normal pH.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **normal pH with abnormal bicarbonate and a high anion gap** signals a mixed disorder. The **delta ratio** (ΔAG/ΔHCO₃⁻) > 2 reveals an additional metabolic alkalosis; < 1 reveals an additional normal-gap acidosis.

## Simplified explanation

Her gap is high (ketoacidosis) but thiazides also make her alkalotic, so the pH looks normal.
hint: Normal pH does not mean normal acid-base status.
